EL Development submits sole bid for Marina Gardens Lane GLS site at $1,243 psf ppr
article:
The Government Land Sales (GLS) tender for a residential site with ground-floor commercial space at Marina Gardens Lane closed on Oct 15. EL Development was the sole bidder, offering $450.1 million, or $1,243 psf per plot ratio (ppr).

That fell well short of analysts’ expectations of three to six bids and a top bid of between $1,350 and $1,650 psf ppr.

“Most GLS sold recently have fetched very high pricing,” says Lim Yew Soon, managing director of EL Development. “Hopefully, with our land price for Marina Gardens Lane site, if awarded, we can create a compelling reason for purchasers to consider residing in this area despite the fact that it is not in the traditional heartland areas.”

Lim adds that residents could also be drawn by the views from some units, the site’s proximity to Gardens by the Bay and Marina South MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, and upcoming developments in the area.

The tender conditions require the developer to set aside commercial space of no more than 150 sq m (1,615 sq ft) on the 1st storey for future residents. Once the development is complete, the MCST will take over and manage the space.

Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, notes that the "subdued participation" reflects a recurring trend for GLS sites in the CBD.

Meanwhile, Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI, attributes the response to the increase in residential GLS land supply, which has "provided developers with a wider range of land acquisition opportunities across different locations and market segments".

Launched for tender on Aug 13, the 99-year leasehold site is the third to be released in the upcoming Marina South precinct. It spans 64,659 sq ft and has a maximum gross floor area of 362,122 sq ft. It can yield about 390 homes, with commercial space on the first storey.

The site is smaller than the adjacent plot, which a Kingsford Group -led consortium won in July 2023. That tender drew four bids, and Kingsford’s top bid was $1.034 billion, or $1,402 psf ppr.

The consortium launched the 937-unit One Marina Gardens on that plot in April 2025. It sold 38.5% of units over its first weekend at an average of $2,953 psf. Based on caveats lodged, the project is now about 72% sold at an average of $2,971 psf.

The second site, a white site at Marina Gardens Crescent – directly opposite One Marina Gardens and the current GLS site –  could yield about 775 homes. When its tender closed in January 2024, it drew a sole bid of $770.46 million, or $984 psf ppr, from a joint venture of GuocoLand, Hong Leong Holdings and TID.

However, URA rejected it the following month as “too low”. The land rate was nearly 30% below the $1,402 psf ppr paid for the Kingsford site.

EL Development's bid of $1,243 psf ppr is also 11.3% lower than the Kingsford Group-led consortium's bid.

Despite this, Huttons’ Yip notes that EL Development’s bid is 26.3% higher than the $984 psf ppr offer for the Marina Gardens Crescent site, and expects the latest site to be awarded.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, notes that One Marina Gardens is the condo within 500m of the latest site, which is the only District 1 plot on the confirmed list for the 2H2026 GLS programme.

Given the limited supply of new homes in the area, he expects the upcoming project to appeal to owner-occupiers seeking a home near the CBD, as well as investors looking to tap rental demand from expatriate professionals.

SRI's Sandrasegeran adds that the sales performance at One Marina Gardens provides an "encouraging indication" of buyer demand in the emerging Marina South precinct.

"If awarded the Marina Gardens Lane site, the submitted land rate of approximately $1,243 psf ppr could provide EL Development with some flexibility in positioning its eventual residential development within the Marina South precinct," he says.

Against this backdrop, Sandrasegeran estimates that the future development could launch at prices averaging between $2,500 psf to $2,600 psf.

Wong Siew Ying, PropNex head of research and content, says the site “has clear strengths”. It is close to the central business district, Marina Bay Financial Centre and Marina Bay Sands , with Gardens by the Bay across the road.

Even so, she says a couple of factors may have weighed on developers. The Marina South precinct is still taking shape. Its MRT station (Marina South) has been built but will not open until the surrounding area is further developed.

More supply is also on the way. The nearby Marina Gardens Crescent site, which can yield about 775 homes, is on the Reserve List. Under URA’s Master Plan 2025, the precinct is slated to deliver more than 10,000 private and public homes over the long term.

“As the precinct is built out and amenities come on stream, we expect developer interest to firm up,” says Wong.

The location may not appeal to local buyers, as there is no primary school within 1km, says Tricia Song, CBRE head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia. Foreign buyers, meanwhile, face a 60% additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD).

“It is also in a relatively new location with limited amenities and a limited pool of upgrader buyers,” she says.

If the site is awarded at EL Development’s top bid of $1,243 psf ppr, Song expects the developer could launch the project at an average of $2,850 to $2,950 psf.

That would put it just below One Marina Gardens, the nearest comparable. Based on CBRE’s analysis of caveats lodged, the 937-unit project is now 72% sold, with a median transacted price of $3,009 psf so far this year.

Nearby, W Residences Marina View, the branded residence on the Marina View white site, has sold 15 units since its July 2025 launch, with a median of $2,660 psf, notes CBRE.

Older 99-year leasehold condos in the Marina Bay and Shenton Way area have changed hands at median prices of $1,829 psf to $2,480 psf, Song observes. They range from The Sail @ Marina Bay, completed in 2008, to Marina One Residences and V on Shenton, both completed in 2017.

title: What I Would Buy Today to Build a Retirement Income Portfolio from Scratch
article:
Many investors aim to build an income stream to fund retirement.
Buying stocks that give yields above 6% is a real temptation.
However, retirement investing needs resilient businesses with sustainable payouts more than immediately maximising today’s income.
Here’s what I would buy if I were building my retirement portfolio today.
What Should a Retirement Portfolio Actually Do?
A retirement portfolio should generally generate dependable income, grow that income, and protect your capital and income.
Hence, focusing on durable businesses and
real estate investment trusts
(REITs) that can pay out through different economic cycles is prudent.
Inflation
means your money will buy less in 20 years, so growing dividends and distributions help preserve your purchasing power.
To protect your capital and income, diversify across sectors and asset classes.
Concentration can increase risks to your dividend paycheck, even if the yield is attractive.
What I Would Buy #1: High-Quality Singapore Dividend Stocks
High-quality Singapore
dividend
stocks are the backbone of a retirement income portfolio.
Invest in established businesses with durable competitive advantages, strong balance sheets, and a reliable payout history.
Offering yields of between 3% and 5%, Singapore banks
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05),
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, have grown their payouts reliably over the years while keeping strong balance sheets.
DBS achieved a record net profit of S$3.08 billion for 2Q2026, 9% higher year on year (YoY), while OCBC reported a net profit of S$4.19 billion for 1H2026, up 13% YoY.
Rising earnings support higher dividends over time.
Quality dividend stocks provide both dependable current income and dividend growth to fight inflation.
Related articles:
3 Dividend Blue Chips Powering the STI’s 2026 Rally
DBS vs OCBC vs UOB: Which Singapore Bank Looks Strongest?
What I Would Buy #2: A Basket of Quality REITs
Commercial REITs like
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, which owns malls and offices, healthcare landlords like
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU), and industrial-focused REITs like
Mapletree Industrial Trust
(SGX: ME8U) are great additions to a retirement portfolio.
REITs typically pay out at least 90% of their taxable income to enjoy tax transparency, making them favourites of Singapore investors.
And while all these sound great, you must understand that gearing, interest costs and debt maturities can affect distribution per unit (DPU).
A REIT’s income is also highly dependent on various factors such as occupancy levels, rental growth, interest rates and capital management.
Avoid concentrating your entire allocation in one sector, as different sectors thrive in different economic environments.
Related articles:
CICT, FCT or Mapletree Industrial Trust: Which REIT Is the Best Buy Today?
Top 4 S-REITs Raising DPU by 10% or More
What I Would Buy #3: Dividend Growth Stocks
Retirement income is a long game.
A low dividend yield today does not mean a low yield in 10 years.
iFAST Corporation Limited
(SGX: AIY) paid a total dividend of S$0.084 per share in FY2025.
The directors expect to propose at least S$0.12 per share for FY2026, an increase of about 43% YoY.
A durable retirement portfolio also should not concentrate solely on local stocks.
To diversify further, look into
US companies
whose businesses have no local equivalent.
Consumer staple company
Procter & Gamble
(NYSE: PG) has a track record of 136 years of continuous dividend payments and 70 consecutive years of dividend increases.
Related article:
Can iFAST Hit Its 3-Year Target to Boost Dividends by 150%?
Why Every Singapore Dividend Investor Should Consider US Growth Stocks
What I Would Keep in Cash and Lower-Risk Assets
Cash and lower-risk assets are needed for expenses and unexpected needs.
A cash buffer prevents the need to sell your stocks during a market downturn to fund expenses.
While lower-risk assets such as Singapore Government Treasury Bills (T-bills) and Singapore Savings Bonds offer lower returns, these investments provide stability to your portfolio and are useful for short-term cash needs.
How I Would Put the Portfolio Together
Assuming I have S$50,000 to invest now, I would split it into different investments to diversify the portfolio:
35% Singapore dividend stocks
30% REITs
20% dividend growth stocks
15% cash and lower-risk assets
You don’t have to invest everything in one go if you are uncomfortable with lump-sum investing.
Using dollar-cost averaging helps to cultivate discipline in regular investing, keeping you invested regardless of market conditions.
Rather than trying to
time the market
, have a clear investment strategy and capital deployment plan.
Reinvesting every dividend and distribution while you are still working helps to accelerate growth of future income, as it buys additional shares and units without extra capital.
The Numbers I Would Monitor Every Year
Portfolio income growth over the years matters more than daily price movements, especially when combating inflation.
Analyse the businesses’ earnings and free cash flow to understand the sustainability of their dividend and DPU growth.
Especially for REITs, I’d pay close attention to gearing, interest costs, and refinancing requirements.
CICT, for example, announced a DPU of S$0.0602 per unit for 1H2026, up 7.1% YoY.
Its gearing of 37.4% sits well below the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) 50% limit, and its interest coverage ratio (ICR) of 3.9x is more than double the 1.5x minimum.
More than anything, paying attention to changes in the underlying business is essential to avoid holding on to deteriorating assets.
What I Would Avoid
Double-digit yields
can hide distress like falling earnings, stressed balance sheets, or unsustainable payouts.
I’d also steer clear of mature businesses bought purely for today’s income, as they have little ability to grow their payouts.
Growing dividends can help your money outpace inflation and maintain purchasing power.
Concentration can increase risks to my dividend paycheck.
While Singapore banks and REITs offer very attractive yields, they cannot be the only holdings in my portfolio.
Get Smart: Build the Income Before You Need It
Starting early to build the income you need for retirement allows compounding to work its magic.
The goal is to build a portfolio that can survive downturns while growing over the years.
Rather than chasing the highest yield today, combining dividend stocks, REITs, dividend growers, and a cash buffer creates a more resilient income stream.
Remember, the best retirement income portfolio is one that keeps paying you long after your salary stops.

title: ECB in no rush to act amid opposing economic forces, Kazaks says
article:
(Oct 15): The European Central Bank can afford to take some time in analysing inflation dynamics that are shaped by opposing forces in the global economy, governing council member Martins Kazaks said.

While the persistent rise in oil and gas prices is set to keep consumer-price growth elevated, the selloff in government debt in recent weeks might start to weigh on economic activity, the Latvian central-bank chief said in an interview.

“My feeling is that the inflationary forces will still be stronger in the immediate future,” Kazaks said in Bangkok, where he’s attending the IMF’s annual meetings. “So the direction of policy is clear, even if there isn’t any immediate need to rush on rates. We’re not behind the curve, so in that sense, we’re well positioned.”

ECB officials are debating what to do next after raising rates twice since the start of the Iran war this year. With inflation approaching 4%, some have said that more tightening might be necessary to return to the 2% target.

Belgian central-bank chief Pierre Wunsch told Bloomberg Television this week that “we are probably going to have to hike again,” even if uncertainty is elevated. His Lithuanian colleague Gediminas Simkus agreed, saying that recent evidence suggests a need for higher borrowing costs.

Kazaks highlighted that risks to inflation on the upside are “still bigger than the risks to growth on the downside.” However, the threats to economic expansion “are at risk of being more nonlinear,” he said.

See also: IMF sees Asia’s growth slowing despite AI-fuelled resilience

Against such a complex backdrop, decision-making at the Frankfurt-based institution could become more complicated as rates breach a level above which they’re estimated to restrict the economy, according to Kazaks.

“The tradeoffs for monetary policy are going to get more tricky,” he said. “So far, the decisions have been relatively easy. But there’s a lot of uncertainty and very low visibility.”

Adding to the challenge is France, which has led the recent bond selloff as the government struggles to reduce its budget deficit. Yields in other highly indebted euro nations have risen as well, raising concerns that market moves hamper the transmission of monetary policy and force the ECB to intervene.

See also: ECB may not have to do as much if markets tighten, Dolenc says

“Unwarranted volatility in financial markets would be a worry, but it doesn’t mean that any stress in financial markets becomes our problem,” Kazaks said. “There’s still time to fix the fiscal issue, and I would urge it to be done.”

The French government has presented plans to narrow its deficit and now needs to prove to nervous financial markets that it can implement them. Speculation about possible ECB intervention has grown after the premium investors demand over equivalent German debt rose to the highest level since the euro-area crisis.

But monetary policy shouldn’t get involved by helping lower French borrowing costs, Kazaks said.

“It’d be very shortsighted and counterproductive to make it the solution to all the problems,” he said.

“Of course, transmission of monetary policy is of interest to us and we will follow that,” he added. “If things become disorderly, we will do what is necessary. But we shouldn’t try to solve every possible problem.”

Kazaks also touched on minimum reserve requirements, a topic that’s lingered for a while.

An increase would remove liquidity from circulation and contribute to quantitative tightening. It would also lower central banks’ interest payments, helping them address losses accrued as a result of quantitative easing.

“If we have a policy case to use it, then we should,” Kazaks said. “We explain it to the market so that our reaction function is understandable, and then it’s going to be alright.”

Lithuania’s Simkus said on Wednesday that “there’s nothing wrong with discussing it” and that the current level isn’t “carved in stone.”
